summary.heading: Energy and its conservation
summary.html:
• Energy (J) is held in stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear. It is transferred by forces doing work, by heating, by electric currents and by waves.
  • Conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy of an isolated system is constant; it only moves between stores or places.
  • Energy is never "lost" or "used up": a braking car's kinetic energy becomes thermal energy in the brakes and surroundings.

summary.heading: Work
summary.html:
$$W = Fs\cos\theta$$
  • Work done by a force is a transfer of energy (1 J of work transfers 1 J). Only the component of the force along the displacement does work. Work is a scalar.
  • $\theta = 0°$: $W = Fs$ (energy into the body). $\theta = 180°$ (friction, braking): $W = -Fs$ (energy out). $\theta = 90°$: $W = 0$ (normal force on a level road, centripetal force).
  • No displacement, no work: holding a bag still does no work on the bag.
  • For a changing force, work = area under the force–displacement graph. For a spring this is a triangle, $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

summary.heading: Kinetic energy and the work–energy principle
summary.html:
$$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$$
  • Doubling the speed quadruples $E_k$ (so the braking distance for the same force is four times longer).
  • Work–energy principle: the work done by the resultant force equals the change in kinetic energy, $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta E_k$.
  • It comes from $Fs = mas$ with $v^2 = 2as$ (starting from rest). Use it to find speeds or distances without finding the acceleration or the time.

summary.heading: Potential energy and conservation of mechanical energy
summary.html:
$$\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \qquad E_H = \tfrac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2$$
  • $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ only near the Earth's surface, where $g$ is constant; any level can be zero, because only changes matter. Far away, use the methods of D.1.
  • Doubling the extension stores four times the elastic energy.
  • Mechanical energy = kinetic + gravitational potential + elastic potential. With no friction or drag it is conserved:
$$\Delta E_k + \Delta E_p + \Delta E_H = 0$$
  • Frictionless slope or ramp, starting from rest: $v = \sqrt{2g\Delta h}$, whatever the mass or the shape of the path. Energy methods solve curved tracks in one line.
  • Non-conservative forces (friction, drag) transfer mechanical energy to thermal energy: the change in mechanical energy equals the (negative) work they do, $\Delta E_{\text{mech}} = W_{\text{friction, drag}}$. So average resistive force = energy "missing" ÷ distance.

summary.heading: Power
summary.html:
$$P = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t} = Fv$$
  • Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy, in watts (1 W = 1 $\text{J s}^{-1}$).
  • At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, so the power needed is $P = Fv$ with $F$ the resistive force.
  • If drag is roughly proportional to $v^2$, the power to overcome it grows as $v^3$: double the speed, about eight times the power.
  • 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ (the energy transferred by 1 kW in one hour).

summary.heading: Efficiency and Sankey diagrams
summary.html:
$$\eta = \frac{\text{useful work out}}{\text{total work in}} = \frac{\text{useful power out}}{\text{total power in}}$$
  • Efficiency has no unit (often a percentage) and can never exceed 1.
  • A Sankey diagram shows transfers as arrows with widths proportional to the energy: input from the left, useful output to the right, wasted energy bending away. The output widths add up to the input.
  • Wasted energy is degraded: spread out as thermal energy in the surroundings, no longer able to do useful work. Mechanical energy can all become thermal energy, but no engine working in a continuous cycle can turn all its thermal energy into work, so every heat engine is well below 100% efficient (B.4).

summary.heading: Energy sources and energy density
summary.html:
• Primary sources occur in nature (coal, oil, gas, uranium, wind, sunlight, flowing water, biomass). Secondary sources (electricity, hydrogen) are made from them and are easier to transport and use.
  • Renewable: replaced naturally as fast as we use them (sunlight, wind, tides). Non-renewable: will run out (fossil fuels, uranium).
QuantityMeaningUnit
Energy densityenergy released per unit volume of fuel$\text{J m}^{-3}$
Specific energyenergy released per unit mass of fuel$\text{J kg}^{-1}$
  • Energy density = specific energy × density of the fuel.
  • Approximate specific energies: wood 16, coal 25–33, petrol 45, methane 55, hydrogen 140 $\text{MJ kg}^{-1}$; a lithium-ion battery under 1 $\text{MJ kg}^{-1}$; uranium-235 (fission) about $8 \times 10^{7}$ $\text{MJ kg}^{-1}$, about a million times more than chemical fuels.
  • Hydrogen and methane have high specific energy but, as gases, low energy density unless compressed.
  • Fuel per day: input power = output ÷ efficiency; energy = power × time; mass = energy ÷ specific energy.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Forgetting $\cos\theta$, or using the wrong angle (it is between the force and the displacement).
  • Thinking every force on a moving body does work: perpendicular forces do none.
  • Doubling $E_k$ (or $E_H$) when the speed (or extension) doubles: it quadruples.
  • Using $mg\Delta h$ far from the Earth's surface.
  • Assuming mechanical energy is conserved when friction or drag act, or when the speed is lower than expected.
  • Saying energy is "lost" rather than transferred.
  • Inverting the efficiency ratio (an answer over 100% is a warning sign).
  • Mixing up energy density (per $\text{m}^3$) and specific energy (per kg).

Theories: Ask students to list every topic they know where energy conservation is used (mechanics, circuits, heating, nuclear). Why does one rule that works everywhere make us trust it more?
Conservation of energy predicts results of experiments nobody has tried yet. Is prediction a better test of a theory than explanation?
Experiments: Joule's falling weights warmed water by a fraction of a degree. What would he have needed to control to make that measurement believable?
Why did it matter that heat and work could be measured in the same unit?
Falsification (or not): Beta decay seemed to break energy conservation, and Pauli proposed an undetectable particle instead. Was this good science or a way of dodging the evidence?
The neutrino was detected 26 years later. Does that success justify the move after the event, or only in hindsight?
Global impact: Use the energy density table: why do aircraft still burn kerosene rather than use batteries?
Physics can compare coal, nuclear and wind on efficiency and energy density. Which important questions about them can it not answer?

oracy.activity: Explain it to a younger student
oracy.html:
Explain it to a younger student (pairs, 6 minutes, then swap roles): one explains; the other plays a curious 12-year-old who keeps asking "why?". Question: "With the same braking force, why does a car going twice as fast need about four times the braking distance?"

  • Think of it like this: …
  • That happens because …
  • So, putting it together, …

Listen for: kinetic energy $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ quadruples, and the work done by the brakes, force × distance, must remove all of it.

Is energy real, or just bookkeeping?: Compare energy with money in a bank account: you never see "the money", only numbers that must add up. Where does the analogy break down?
Can something be real if we can only calculate it, never observe it directly?
How fundamental is a fundamental idea?: $E = mc^2$ made mass a store of energy. Did the meaning of "energy" change, or did we just find a new store?
Can students name another basic idea that was redefined (the atom, the planet, the metre)? What happened to the old knowledge?
When should a theory be defended rather: Compare Pauli's neutrino with the search for the "ether" (A.5). One rescue worked and one failed. What was different?
How long should scientists wait for a predicted particle before giving up?
Does language shape knowledge?: Collect everyday uses of "work", "power" and "energy" ("I've no energy today"). Which help and which mislead in physics?
Is it better for science to invent new words or to give special meanings to old ones?
Who should decide?: Give the class a short energy decision (a new power station near the school). What knowledge, besides physics, would a good decision need?
Should scientists give advice only, or also say what they think should be done?

videos.title: What is energy?
videos.use: Don Lincoln on what physicists mean by energy and how that differs from everyday use. A good starter for the ToK questions "Is energy real, or just bookkeeping?" and "Does language shape knowledge?".

videos.title: The Most Misunderstood Concept in Physics
videos.use: Extension (about 27 minutes): if energy is always conserved, why can't we reuse it? Links degraded energy and efficiency to entropy in B.4. Show selected parts in class or share with keen students.

videos.title: The Biggest Misconception in Physics
videos.use: Extension (about 28 minutes): why energy conservation comes from a symmetry of nature, and where it stops applying on cosmic scales. Good for able students and for the ToK question "How fundamental is a fundamental idea?".

alsoLabs.note: Students calculate the kinetic energy before and after each collision and explosion, and the fraction transferred to other stores. The lab's main topic is A.2.
